Lesson 6

  
Many Things at Once: Fibers

  
One cook can keep many recipes going by using bookmarks, and can cleanly stop any of them. Effect calls a bookmark in a running recipe a fiber. Fibers let you run recipes side by side, race them, and interrupt them, which Promises can't do.


  
The story

  
Remember: still one cook, Sam. Sam is making three smoothies for three customers. Sam does not grow extra arms.

  

    

      
      
Bookmarks. Sam puts a bookmark in recipe 1 while it blends, starts recipe 2, bookmarks that, starts recipe 3. Three recipes in progress, one cook.

    

    

      
      
Each bookmark is a fiber. It remembers where in the recipe we were, so Sam can pick it back up when the bell rings.

    

    

      
      
Customer 2 leaves. With a receipt, too bad, the smoothie gets made anyway. With a fiber, Sam pulls the bookmark out. Effect calls this interruption.

    

  


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code

  
Run several cards at once. Effect.all takes a list of cards and gives back one card that produces a list of results. The concurrency option is "how many bookmarks may Sam have open at once."


import { Effect } from "effect"

const makeSmoothie = (name: string) =>
  Effect.sleep("3 seconds").pipe(Effect.as(`${name} 🥤`))

const three = Effect.all(
  [makeSmoothie("mango"), makeSmoothie("berry"), makeSmoothie("kiwi")],
  { concurrency: "unbounded" }      // as many bookmarks as needed
)
// three : Effect<string[]>

Effect.runPromise(three).then(console.log)   // ~3 seconds, not 9

  
Race. Two cards start; the first to finish wins, and the loser is interrupted (its bookmark is pulled).


const fastest = Effect.race(makeSmoothie("mango"), makeSmoothie("berry"))

  
A bookmark you can hold. Effect.forkChild starts a card in the background and hands you the fiber. Fiber.join waits for it. Fiber.interrupt stops it.


import { Effect, Fiber, Console } from "effect"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const fiber = yield* Effect.forkChild(makeSmoothie("mango"))   // start it, keep the bookmark
  yield* Console.log("customer is waiting...")
  yield* Effect.sleep("1 second")
  yield* Console.log("customer left!")
  yield* Fiber.interrupt(fiber)                                  // pull the bookmark
  yield* Console.log("stopped the mango smoothie")
})

Effect.runPromise(program)

  
Try that with a Promise. There is no way to stop orderSmoothie("mango") once it's called.


  

    
Three smoothies, one cook

    
Each smoothie takes 3 seconds of blending. Pick how many bookmarks Sam may hold, start, and time it. While it runs, customer 2 can leave.

    

      
        
        
        
      
      
      
      elapsed: 0.0 s
    

    

      
    

    

  


  

  
Check yourself

  
1. Did Sam ever do two things at the exact same instant? Then how did three smoothies take three seconds?No. Sam only did the short steps. The blenders did the long waiting parts, all overlapping, while Sam held three bookmarks.

  
2. What is a fiber, in kitchen words?A bookmark in a half-finished recipe: it remembers where Sam was, so Sam can come back to it, or pull it out.

  
3. A customer leaves. What happens to their smoothie with a Promise? With a fiber?Promise: it gets made anyway; nothing can stop it. Fiber: Sam interrupts it, the recipe stops at its next step, and any cleanup it promised still runs.

  
4. In Effect.all with concurrency: 2, how long do three 3-second smoothies take?About 6 seconds. Two run together (3 s), then the third runs alone (3 s). Try it in the demo above.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • The word for "many things in progress at once" is concurrency. It's not "many things happening at the same instant," which is parallelism and needs more cooks. Say "in progress," never "at the same time," and you'll avoid a year of confusion.
    • 
      
  • Effect.forkChild makes the fiber a child of the current one. If the parent finishes or is interrupted, the child is interrupted too. Effect 4 also has forkScoped and forkDetach for other lifetimes; skip them.
    • 
      
  • Leaving out concurrency means one at a time.
    • 
      
  • Interruption is polite. A fiber isn't killed mid-instruction; it stops at the next step boundary and runs its cleanup. Compare pulling the plug to pressing the off button.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 5Lesson 7: Cleaning up →


  





  
Lesson 7

  
Cleaning Up

  
Whatever you borrow, you give back, even when things go wrong. Effect has a built-in rule for "get a thing, use it, always put it back," and it holds no matter how the recipe ends: success, error, or interruption.


  
The story

  
Maya checks a book out of the library. Three ways her afternoon can go.

  

    

      
      
She reads it and returns it. The happy ending.

    

    

      
      
She spills juice on chapter three. An error. She still has to return it.

    

    

      
      
She's called home mid-chapter. An interruption. She still returns the book on the way out.

    

  

  
The return is not optional. It doesn't care why she stopped reading. Kitchen version: Sam turns on the blender. Whether the smoothie succeeds, the fruit was rotten, or the customer left and the recipe was interrupted, the blender gets turned off. A blender left running overnight is how kitchens burn down. Effect calls this pattern acquire and release, and the guarantee is: release always runs.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Effect, Console } from "effect"

const blenderOn  = Console.log("blender ON  🔛")
const blenderOff = Console.log("blender OFF ⏹️")

const useBlender = Effect.acquireRelease(
  blenderOn,            // acquire
  () => blenderOff      // release: ALWAYS runs
)

const smoothie = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* useBlender
  yield* Console.log("blending...")
  yield* Effect.fail(new Error("rotten fruit!"))   // uh oh
  yield* Console.log("pouring")                    // never reached
})

Effect.runPromise(Effect.scoped(smoothie)).catch(() => {})
// blender ON  🔛
// blending...
// blender OFF ⏹️        <-- ran anyway

  
Delete the Effect.fail line and you'll see ON, blending, pouring, OFF. Put it back: ON, blending, OFF. Either way, OFF.


  

    
Three endings, one release

    
Choose how the recipe ends, then run it. Watch the last line of the log and the blender.

    

      
        
        
        
      
      
    

    

      
      

    

  


  
What's Effect.scoped?

  
The library book has a due date: how long you're allowed to keep it. Effect calls that window a scope. Effect.acquireRelease adds "Needs: a Scope" to the card's third line, because the card needs to know when to return things. Effect.scoped says "the scope is this recipe: return everything when it ends." Layers (Lesson 5) also make scopes, so a blender acquired in a layer is returned when the app shuts down.

  
You don't need to understand scopes deeply this month. You need: acquireRelease borrows, scoped sets the due date, release always happens.


  
Why this is a big deal

  
With a Promise, there's no "interrupted" path at all, so people forget cleanup on the "customer left" case, because that case doesn't exist for them. Then a real program runs for a week and has ten thousand blenders still on. Effect makes the interrupted path a first-class thing, and cleanup runs on it too.


  
Check yourself

  
1. Name the three ways a recipe can end. Which of them skips the release step?Success, error, interruption. None of them skip release.

  
2. Why is "turn the blender off" not just the last line of the recipe?Because if a line before it fails or gets interrupted, the last line is never reached. Release has to be attached to the borrowing, not written at the end.

  
3. In library words, what's a scope?The due date: the window of time you're allowed to hold what you borrowed.

  
4. A friend says "I'll just put cleanup in the .catch of my Promise." What case did they forget?The interrupted case. Promises don't have one, so their cleanup never runs when a customer walks away.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • acquireRelease(acquire, release) returns the acquired thing, so you can do const blender = yield* useBlender and then use it. The example throws it away for simplicity.
    • 
      
  • Effect.ensuring(cleanup) is the simpler cousin: "after this card, always run cleanup." Effect.addFinalizer registers cleanup from inside a gen block.
    • 
      
  • A closer for the unit: draw the full smoothie card on the board with all three lines filled in, a retry and timeout wrapped around it, a Blender layer provided, and acquireRelease keeping the blender safe. Then ask: "What can go wrong that we haven't written down?" The answer, "a defect, and we'd see it loudly," is the whole philosophy in one sentence.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 6Unit 2, Lesson 8: Schedules →


  





  
Lesson 8

  
The Kitchen Routine

  
A schedule is a little plan for when to do something again. It lives on its own, separate from any recipe card, so you can snap the same schedule onto any card. Snap it on with retry to try again after a failure, or with repeat to go again after a success.


  
The story

  
Sam is waiting for a box of mangoes. The truck is late.

  

    

      
      
The mangoes are late. Sam could stand at the back door and stare, or check it every two seconds forever. Both are bad plans.

    

    

      
      
Ty tapes a routine to the wall. It doesn't say how to check the door or wipe a counter. Only when to go again, and when to stop.

    

    

      
      
Sam follows the chart. Knock again because it went wrong. Wipe again because it went right. Same idea, any card.

    

  

  
There are two kinds of "again" on that chart. Again because it went wrong: the box wasn't there, so check later. That's retry, from Lesson 4. Again because it went right: the counter is clean, and in 10 minutes it gets wiped again. That's called repeat. And the routine chart itself has a programmer name: a schedule.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Effect, Console, Schedule, Data } from "effect"

class NotHereYet extends Data.TaggedError("NotHereYet") {}

// Again on SUCCESS: repeat
const wipe = Console.log("🧽 wipe the counter")
const wipeThreeTimes = Effect.repeat(wipe, Schedule.recurs(2))   // 1 + 2 more

// Again on FAILURE: retry
let knocks = 0
const checkDelivery = Effect.gen(function* () {
  knocks++
  if (knocks < 4) {
    yield* Console.log(`knock ${knocks}... not here yet`)
    return yield* Effect.fail(new NotHereYet())
  }
  yield* Console.log(`knock ${knocks}... 📦 here!`)
  return "mangoes"
})
const keepChecking = Effect.retry(checkDelivery, Schedule.spaced("100 millis"))

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* wipeThreeTimes
  const box = yield* keepChecking
  yield* Console.log(`got ${box}`)
})

Effect.runPromise(program)
// 🧽 wipe the counter
// 🧽 wipe the counter
// 🧽 wipe the counter
// knock 1... not here yet
// knock 2... not here yet
// knock 3... not here yet
// knock 4... 📦 here!
// got mangoes

  
Schedule.recurs(2) means "2 more times." The card always runs once first, so that's 3 wipes. Schedule.spaced("100 millis") means "wait 100 milliseconds, then go again." It has no limit, so the knocking only stops because the box finally showed up.


  
Three rules for the chart

  

    

      
The chart saysIn codeThe waits

      
        
"Every 10 minutes"Schedule.spaced("10 minutes")10, 10, 10, 10 ... forever

        
"1 minute, then 2, then 4"Schedule.exponential("1 minute")1, 2, 4, 8 ... doubling forever

        
"At most 3 more times"Schedule.recurs(3)no waiting, but stops after 3

      
    

  

  
Notice that the first two never stop on their own. A schedule that says "doubling forever" is a schedule for a very patient cook.


  
Two rules at once

  
Ty's real chart says both "1, then 2, then 4" and "give up after 3 extra checks." You can glue two schedules together with Schedule.max:


const routine = Schedule.max([
  Schedule.exponential("100 millis"),   // wait 100, 200, 400 ...
  Schedule.recurs(3)                    // ...but only 3 more tries
])

const patient = Effect.retry(checkDelivery, routine).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("NotHereYet", () => Console.log("gave up, call the farm 📞"))
)
// knock at 0 ms... not here yet
// knock at 100 ms... not here yet
// knock at 300 ms... not here yet
// knock at 700 ms... not here yet
// gave up, call the farm 📞

  
(Here the truck never comes, and each knock prints the time.) Read Schedule.max as "follow both rules." Sam only goes again if both rules say yes, so the moment recurs(3) says "that's enough," it stops. And when the two rules want different waits, Sam waits the longer one, the max.

  
Look at the gaps: 100, then 200, then 400. That's the doubling. After the last try, the error NotHereYet is still on the card's "Can go wrong" line, because a schedule can give up. So we wrote a plan for it with catchTag, just like Lesson 4.


  

    
Tape a routine to the wall

    
Pick a routine and whether Sam is knocking (retry) or wiping (repeat), then run it. Each dot is one run of the card. Watch the gaps.

    

      
        
        
        
        
      
    

    

      
        
        
      
      
        
        
        
      
      
    

    

    

      
    

    

  


  
Check yourself

  
1. Sam wipes the counter, and it works. Which one makes Sam wipe again: retry or repeat?repeat. It goes again after a success. retry would stop right there, because the wipe didn't fail.

  
2. With Effect.retry(card, Schedule.recurs(3)), what is the most times the card can run?4 times: the first run, plus 3 more. The schedule only counts the "agains."

  
3. Why does a kitchen use "wait 1, then 2, then 4" for a late truck instead of "check every second"?Checking every second wastes the cook's time and bugs whoever you're asking. Short waits first catch a truck that's only a little late; longer waits later stop you from pestering when it's very late. Real servers use this so a thousand phones don't all knock at once.

  
4. A friend writes Effect.retry(card, Schedule.spaced("1 second")) and the card fails every single time. What happens? How would you fix it?It knocks once a second, forever. spaced never says stop. Fix: follow two rules, like Schedule.max([Schedule.spaced("1 second"), Schedule.recurs(5)]), then plan for the error that comes out when it gives up.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • The key idea is separation: the card says what to do, the schedule says when to do it again. Same split as Lesson 3 (plan vs. running). Ask: "Could we tape the delivery chart next to a different card, like calling a friend back?" Yes, that's the point.
    • 
      
  • retry only goes again on failure; on success it hands back the value right away. repeat only goes again on success; the first failure stops it and the error comes out. repeat gives back the schedule's output (for recurs, a count), not the card's value. Mention it only if asked.
    • 
      
  • "Doubling waits" is called exponential backoff by grown-ups. Servers use it so that a thousand phones don't all knock at the same second. Schedule.jittered adds a little randomness for the same reason. Mention it, don't teach it.
    • 
      
  • Schedule.min([a, b]) is the opposite of max: keep going while either rule says yes, and wait the shorter gap. Handy for "doubling, but never more than 10 seconds."
    • 
      
  • Shortcuts students may see in real code: Effect.retry(card, { schedule, times: 3 }) and Schedule.upTo({ times: 3 }), which add a limit without writing max. Lesson 4's { times: 3 } is the same idea with no waiting between tries.
    • 
      
  • Waiting in a schedule is a fiber waiting (Lesson 6). The cook isn't frozen; other bookmarks keep going.
    • 
      
  • In Lesson 14 we'll test schedules without actually waiting, by fast-forwarding a pretend clock.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 7Lesson 9: Shared state →


  





  
Lesson 9

  
The Whiteboard, Shared State

  
When several bookmarks share one number, keep it on a whiteboard where "read it, change it, write it back" is one step nobody can cut into. Effect calls that whiteboard a Ref. It fixes a sneaky bug where sales go missing even though nobody made a mistake you can see.


  
The story

  
The kitchen has a whiteboard by the door. On it: Smoothies sold today: 0. Every time a smoothie goes out, the tally goes up by one. Remember Lesson 6: Sam is one cook with several bookmarks, and three orders are in progress.

  

    

      
      
Three orders, three looks. Each order checks the board and remembers "0."

    

    

      
      
Bookmarks while pouring. Pouring takes a while. Sam's memory of "0" gets older and older.

    

    

      
      
Three sold. The board says 1. Each order wrote "what I remembered, plus one."

    

  

  
Two sales vanished, and every single step looked fine. The problem is the gap. Between "look" and "write," Sam put the bookmark down, and the number Sam remembered went stale. Programmers call this a lost update.

  
The fix: a whiteboard rule. "Read it, add one, write it back" happens in one step, with no gap for a bookmark. Effect's whiteboard is called a Ref, and that one step is called Ref.update.

  
Ty, the kitchen manager, has a job here too. Ty checks the label on the whiteboard: "numbers only." Try to write "banana" on it and Ty stops you before the kitchen opens.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code

  
A Ref is made, read, overwritten, and updated. Each of those is a recipe card, so you yield* them.


import { Effect, Console, Ref } from "effect"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const board = yield* Ref.make(0)          // a whiteboard that says 0

  yield* Ref.set(board, 5)                  // wipe it, write 5
  yield* Ref.update(board, (n) => n + 1)    // read, add 1, write back: one step

  const sold = yield* Ref.get(board)        // look at it
  yield* Console.log(`smoothies sold: ${sold}`)
})

Effect.runPromise(program)
// smoothies sold: 6

  
board has the type Ref<number>. That's the "numbers only" label Ty checks.


  
Watch the sales vanish

  
Same whiteboard, two ways to sell. The sloppy way reads, pauses, then writes. The safe way uses Ref.update. Three orders run at once, as three fibers.


import { Effect, Console, Ref } from "effect"

// The sloppy way: read, pause, write back what you remember
const sellSloppy = (board: Ref.Ref<number>) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const seen = yield* Ref.get(board)      // read the whiteboard
    yield* Effect.sleep("1 second")         // go pour the smoothie 🥤
    yield* Ref.set(board, seen + 1)         // write back: seen + 1
  })

// The safe way: the read-change-write is ONE step
const sellSafe = (board: Ref.Ref<number>) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    yield* Effect.sleep("1 second")         // go pour the smoothie 🥤
    yield* Ref.update(board, (n) => n + 1)  // nobody can cut in
  })

const busyMinute = (sell: (board: Ref.Ref<number>) => Effect.Effect<void>) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const board = yield* Ref.make(0)        // a fresh whiteboard
    yield* Effect.all(
      [sell(board), sell(board), sell(board)],
      { concurrency: "unbounded" }          // three bookmarks at once
    )
    const sold = yield* Ref.get(board)
    yield* Console.log(`3 smoothies sold, whiteboard says ${sold}`)
  })

Effect.runPromise(
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    yield* busyMinute(sellSloppy)
    yield* busyMinute(sellSafe)
  })
)
// 3 smoothies sold, whiteboard says 1    <-- lost two sales!
// 3 smoothies sold, whiteboard says 3    <-- correct

  
Notice: the sloppy way also uses a Ref. A Ref doesn't save you if you split "read" and "write" into two steps with a pause between them. The magic is in Ref.update, which never leaves a gap.


  

    
Where did the sales go?

    
Three orders share one whiteboard. Pick how each order writes its sale, then run it. Watch what each order remembers.

    

      
        
        
      
      
    

    

      
    

    

  


  
A fresh whiteboard every run

  
Ref.make(0) is a recipe card too: "get a new whiteboard that says 0." So every time you run a recipe that makes one, you get a brand new whiteboard. In the code above, busyMinute runs twice and the second run starts at 0, not at 1. Monday's tally doesn't leak into Tuesday.


  
Check yourself

  
1. Three smoothies went out, and the whiteboard says 1. In kitchen words, what went wrong?Each order remembered an old number ("0") during the pause, then wrote "0 + 1" back, erasing the other orders' marks.

  
2. JavaScript has one cook. So how can two orders "cut in" on each other at all?Bookmarks. During the pause Sam puts one order down and picks up another, so the gap between "look" and "write" is real even with one cook.

  
3. Why does the sloppy seller lose sales even though it uses a Ref?It reads with Ref.get, pauses, then writes with Ref.set. That's still two steps with a gap. Only Ref.update glues them into one.

  
4. You run a recipe that starts with Ref.make(0) two times. Does the second run start at 0, or where the first run left off?At 0. Ref.make is a recipe card, so each run makes a new whiteboard.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • Be honest about one cook. A plain count++ in JavaScript is never torn in half. The bug only appears when a recipe reads, then pauses (yield* of a sleep, an await, a network call), then writes back. A sharp kid may notice that removing the sleep from sellSloppy gives 3. True today, but don't rely on it: Effect may also switch fibers between any two yield* steps to be fair. Ref.update is the guarantee.
    • 
      
  • Grown-up terms: this is a race condition, specifically a lost update or "read-modify-write" bug. A Ref is a mutable reference whose updates are atomic (all at once, never half done).
    • 
      
  • Ref.updateAndGet(board, f) updates and hands back the new number in the same step. Ref.modify updates and returns something else, like a ticket number: Ref.modify(board, (n) => [n + 1, n + 1]). Mention, don't teach.
    • 
      
  • SynchronizedRef is for when the update itself is a card (it needs to wait, like asking the fridge first): SynchronizedRef.updateEffect. Other updaters wait in line while it runs. SubscriptionRef is a whiteboard you can watch: it gives a stream of every new value (Stream is Lesson 11).
    • 
      
  • "Why not just a global let count = 0?" Three reasons: it is shared by every run of the program (no fresh whiteboard, so tests leak into each other); it doesn't show up in any type; and it has the same lost-update gap anyway. A Ref is made inside the recipe and passed where it's needed.
    • 
      
  • Lesson 10 (Queues) is the next step: instead of everyone writing on one board, orders are passed from one bookmark to another on a shelf.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 8: SchedulesLesson 10: Queues →


  





  
Lesson 10

  
The Order Shelf, Queues

  
A queue is a shelf between two fibers: one side puts orders on, the other side takes them off, in order. Whoever finds the shelf empty, or full, waits. And waiting is a bookmark, not a frozen kitchen.


  
The story

  
Lunch rush. Maya and eleven friends line up at the counter. Taking an order is quick: ten seconds. Making a smoothie is slow: a whole minute in the blender.

  

    

      
      
One order at a time. Sam takes an order, then blends it. The whole line stands still for a minute per person.

    

    

      
      
The order shelf. The front counter puts a slip on one end. The blending station takes the oldest slip off the other end.

    

    

      
      
Full shelf? The counter waits. It has two slots. The next slip goes on only when the blender takes one off.

    

  

  
Remember Lesson 6: still one cook. The front counter is one recipe with a bookmark, the blending station is another. Sam hops between them whenever one of them has to wait. Two kinds of waiting can happen:

  
    
    
  • The shelf is empty. The blending station has nothing to do. It puts in a bookmark and waits for a slip. Sam goes and takes orders meanwhile. Nothing freezes.
    • 
    
  • The shelf is full. It only has two slots. The front counter says "one second, please" and waits until the blending station takes a slip off. Then the next slip goes on.
    • 
  

  
That second kind is important. The full shelf pushes back on the front counter, so the kitchen never ends up with 500 slips and 3 bananas. Programmers call that push backpressure.

  
Programmers call the shelf itself a queue. Ty, the kitchen manager, checks what goes on it: if it's an order shelf, only order slips go on. Try to put a shoe there and Ty stops you before the kitchen opens.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Effect, Queue, Console, Fiber } from "effect"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const shelf = yield* Queue.bounded<string>(2)   // a shelf with 2 slots

  const cashier = Effect.gen(function* () {
    for (const order of ["mango", "berry", "kiwi", "lime"]) {
      yield* Queue.offer(shelf, order)             // put (waits if full)
      yield* Console.log(`cashier: ${order} is on the shelf`)
    }
  })

  const blender = Effect.gen(function* () {
    for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
      const order = yield* Queue.take(shelf)       // take (waits if empty)
      yield* Effect.sleep("1 second")              // blending takes a while
      yield* Console.log(`blender: ${order} smoothie 🥤`)
    }
  })

  const front = yield* Effect.forkChild(cashier)   // bookmark 1
  const back = yield* Effect.forkChild(blender)    // bookmark 2
  yield* Fiber.join(front)
  yield* Fiber.join(back)
})

Effect.runPromise(program)
// cashier: mango is on the shelf
// cashier: berry is on the shelf
// cashier: kiwi is on the shelf
// blender: mango smoothie 🥤
// cashier: lime is on the shelf     <-- waited a whole second for a free slot
// blender: berry smoothie 🥤
// blender: kiwi smoothie 🥤
// blender: lime smoothie 🥤

  
Read the log slowly. Mango and berry fill both slots. Kiwi gets on because the blender already grabbed mango off the shelf and into the jar. Then the shelf is full again, so lime waits, the cashier's bookmark stays put, until mango is done and the blender takes berry.

  
The recipe-card lines still work. Queue.bounded<string>(2) is a card that gives you a shelf for strings. Queue.take(shelf) is a card that gives you a string. Neither has anything on the "can go wrong" line.


  

    
Run the lunch rush

    
Eight orders. The cashier takes one every half second. Pick the shelf size, how many blenders, and how fast they blend. Watch who waits.

    

      
        
        
        
      
      
        
        
      
      
        
        
      
      
    

    

      
    

    

  


  
Two blenders, one shelf

  
Add a second blending station. Both take from the same shelf, and each slip goes to exactly one of them, never both.


const blender = (name: string) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
      const order = yield* Queue.take(shelf)
      yield* Effect.sleep("1 second")
      yield* Console.log(`${name}: ${order} smoothie 🥤`)
    }
  })

const left = yield* Effect.forkChild(blender("left blender"))
const right = yield* Effect.forkChild(blender("right blender"))
// ...cashier forked and every fiber joined, same as before
// left blender: mango smoothie 🥤
// right blender: berry smoothie 🥤
// left blender: kiwi smoothie 🥤
// right blender: lime smoothie 🥤

  
Four smoothies in about two seconds instead of four. Still one cook: the blenders do the waiting, and Sam just keeps two bookmarks open.


  
Check yourself

  
1. The blending station finds the shelf empty. What does it do? Does the rest of the kitchen freeze?It waits for a slip, with a bookmark in its recipe. Nothing freezes: Sam goes off and takes orders, and the blender's recipe picks up again the moment a slip lands on the shelf.

  
2. The shelf has 2 slots, but the log shows three orders on the shelf before the first smoothie. How?The blender already took mango off the shelf and put it in the jar. That freed a slot, so kiwi went on. Only two slips were ever on the shelf at once.

  
3. What is backpressure, in kitchen words? Why is it a good thing that the cashier has to wait?The full shelf pushing back on the front counter: "no room, wait a second." It's good because otherwise orders pile up faster than they can be made, and the kitchen drowns in slips it can't finish.

  
4. With two blenders and four one-second orders, how long does it take? Did we add a second cook?About two seconds. No new cook: the blenders do the slow part, and Sam just keeps one more bookmark open.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • Grown-up words: the cashier is the producer, the blender is the consumer, and "first on, first off" is FIFO (first in, first out). Use them after the picture lands, not before.
    • 
      
  • Other shelf shapes, worth a mention: Queue.unbounded() has no limit, so offer never waits (and the slips can pile up forever). Queue.sliding(n): when full, the new slip goes on and the oldest falls off. Queue.dropping(n): when full, the new slip is thrown away. In those two, offer hands back false when a slip didn't make it.
    • 
      
  • Why the loops count to 4: a real kitchen loops forever (Effect.forever) and stops by interruption (Lesson 6) or by closing the shelf. Closing: make it with Queue.bounded<string, Cause.Done>(n) and call Queue.end(shelf). Slips already on the shelf can still be taken, then take fails with Done. That's what the queue's second type slot is for. Queue.shutdown is the rude version: it throws away whatever is left.
    • 
      
  • If a kid asks "can everyone hear every order?": that's PubSub, the loudspeaker. Each listener calls PubSub.subscribe (it needs a Scope, Lesson 7) and every listener gets every message from PubSub.publish. A queue hands each slip to exactly one taker.
    • 
      
  • Deferred is the pickup bell: a one-time slot that is filled once (Deferred.succeed) and wakes everyone waiting on Deferred.await. Nice for "start when the kitchen opens."
    • 
      
  • Contrast with Lesson 9: the whiteboard (Ref) holds one current value anyone can read again. The shelf holds a line of things, and taking one removes it. Lesson 11's conveyor belt can be fed straight from a queue (Stream.fromQueue).
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 9: Shared stateLesson 11: Streams →


  





  
Lesson 11

  
The Conveyor Belt, Streams

  
A recipe card hands you one thing. A stream hands you many things, one after another, maybe forever. And a stream is still a plan: nothing moves until you run it.


  
The story

  
Sam's kitchen gets a new toy: a sushi-style conveyor belt. Fruit rides along it, one piece at a time.

  

    

      
      
Sam builds a fruit belt. Three stations: wash every fruit, toss the bruised ones, and "only the first 5, please."

    

    

      
      
Maya reaches, the belt clicks forward. She doesn't reach, nothing moves.

    

    

      
      
After five, the belt stops for good. The bin behind it never runs out, and it doesn't matter.

    

  

  
Programmers call a belt like this a stream. Because the person at the end does the reaching, they say it is pull-based: the end pulls fruit, the belt doesn't shove it.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Console, Effect, Stream } from "effect"

const belt = Stream.make("🥭", "🍓", "🍌", "🥝")   // four fruit on the belt
// belt : Stream<string, never, never>

const washed = belt.pipe(
  Stream.map((fruit) => fruit + "💧")               // the wash station
)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const tray = yield* Stream.runCollect(washed)     // run the belt, keep everything
  yield* Console.log(tray)
})

Effect.runPromise(program)
// [ '🥭💧', '🍓💧', '🍌💧', '🥝💧' ]

  
Stream.make puts fruit on the belt. Have an array already? Stream.fromIterable(["🥭", "🍓"]) does the same. .pipe(...) adds stations, in order. Stream.runCollect is Maya with a tray: she runs the belt to the end and hands back an array of everything that arrived.


  
The same three lines

  
Look at that type: Stream<string, never, never>. Three slots, the same three lines as a recipe card (Lesson 3):

  
Stream<A, E, R>

  

    

      
LineOn a card Effect<A, E, R>On a belt Stream<A, E, R>

      
        
You getone Amany As, one at a time

        
Can go wrongEE (a fruit falls off and the belt stops)

        
NeedsRR (services, like Lesson 5)

      
    

  

  
And running it turns the belt back into a card: Stream.runCollect(washed) is an Effect<Array<string>, never, never>. You yield* it like any other card.


  
An endless belt

  
Now a fruit bin that never runs out. We add a little window, Stream.tap, so we can watch every time the belt moves.


const endlessBelt = Stream.iterate(1, (n) => n + 1)   // fruit #1, #2, #3, ... forever

const firstFive = endlessBelt.pipe(
  Stream.tap((n) => Console.log(`belt moves: fruit #${n}`)),  // a window to watch the belt
  Stream.filter((n) => n % 3 !== 0),          // toss station: every 3rd fruit is bruised
  Stream.map((n) => `  washed fruit #${n} 💧`), // wash station
  Stream.take(5)                              // "only the first 5, please"
)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* Stream.runForEach(firstFive, (fruit) => Console.log(fruit))
  yield* Console.log("belt stopped. done! 🎉")
})

Effect.runPromise(program)
// belt moves: fruit #1
//   washed fruit #1 💧
// belt moves: fruit #2
//   washed fruit #2 💧
// belt moves: fruit #3        <-- bruised, tossed
// belt moves: fruit #4
//   washed fruit #4 💧
// belt moves: fruit #5
//   washed fruit #5 💧
// belt moves: fruit #6        <-- bruised, tossed
// belt moves: fruit #7
//   washed fruit #7 💧
// belt stopped. done! 🎉

  
An endless belt, and the program finishes. Count the "belt moves" lines: seven. Fruit #8 never moves, because nobody asked for it. That's pull-based. Stream.runForEach is a different Maya: instead of filling a tray, she does something with each fruit as it arrives.

  
Try the same thing with a plain array and you'd have to build the whole endless array first. You'd be waiting forever.


  

    
The fruit belt

    
Turn stations on or off, then pull. Every third fruit is bruised. Watch the "pulled from bin" counter: it only goes up when Maya asks.

    

      
      
      
    

    

      
      
      
      
      pulled from bin: 0 · on tray: 0
    

    

      
    

    

  


  
Check yourself

  
1. An Effect hands you one thing. What does a stream hand you?Many things, one after another, maybe forever.

  
2. Which station tosses bruised fruit, map or filter? Which one washes?filter tosses (it keeps or drops each fruit). map washes (it changes each fruit into a new one).

  
3. The belt is endless, but the program above stops. Why? How many fruit actually moved?take(5) stops asking after five, and nothing upstream moves without being asked. Seven fruit moved: five kept, two bruised ones tossed. Fruit #8 never moved.

  
4. You write const belt = Stream.make("🥭", "🍓") and nothing prints, nothing moves. Is that a bug?No. A stream is a plan, like a recipe card. Nothing moves until a run... function, like Stream.runCollect, runs it.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • "Pull-based" vs "push-based": a Promise or an event listener pushes values at you whether you're ready or not. A pull-based stream waits for the consumer. That's also how backpressure from Lesson 10 shows up here: a slow Maya just means a slow belt, never a pile of fruit on the floor.
    • 
      
  • A sharp kid may ask "is it really one fruit at a time?" Honest answer: under the hood Effect moves fruit in small batches (it calls them chunks) to be fast. The rules still behave like one at a time: take(5) gives exactly five, and an endless belt still stops.
    • 
      
  • Other ways to build a belt: Stream.range(1, 10), Stream.tick("1 second") (an endless belt that clicks once a second), Stream.fromSchedule(...) using the schedules from Lesson 8, Stream.fromEffectSchedule(card, schedule) for "check the oven every 30 seconds."
    • 
      
  • Stream.mapEffect(f, { concurrency: 4 }) is a station that runs a whole recipe card per fruit, several at once (Lesson 6's bookmarks, still one cook).
    • 
      
  • Stream.fromQueue(shelf) turns Lesson 10's order shelf into a belt: whatever lands on the shelf rides the belt. Stream.fromPubSub does the same for a PubSub.
    • 
      
  • A Sink is the grown-up word for "whoever is at the end of the belt." Stream.run(stream, Sink.sum) adds up numbers. runCollect, runForEach, runFold, runDrain are the common ones.
    • 
      
  • Async iterables (for await) are JavaScript's built-in belt. Stream.fromAsyncIterable and Stream.toAsyncIterable convert both ways.
    • 
      
  • In v4, runCollect gives a plain Array. Older Effect (v2/v3) gave a Chunk, so old blog posts may look different.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 10: QueuesLesson 12: Schema →


  





  
Lesson 12

  
Checking the Delivery

  
Anything that comes from outside the kitchen gets checked at the back door. Effect lets you write down what a delivery should look like, once. That one description does two jobs: it checks the real delivery while the kitchen is running, and it tells Ty what a good delivery looks like.


  
The story

  
Every morning a truck pulls up to the back door with crates of fruit. Sam didn't pack those crates. Sam has never met the driver.

  

    

      
      
A truck at the back door. The crate says "mango." It might be full of bananas. It might be empty.

    

    

      
      
Ty can't help here. Ty checks the recipe cards before the kitchen opens. The truck arrives after, while the kitchen is running.

    

    

      
      
The packing list. Sam checks each box on the list. A good crate goes on the shelf. A bad one gets a slip saying exactly which box was wrong.

    

  

  
The packing list taped by the back door says: Crate of fruit. fruit: the word "mango" or the word "berry". count: a whole number above 0. An inspector checks each box on the list against the real crate. If everything matches, the crate goes on the shelf, and from then on everyone can trust it. If anything is wrong, the crate stays on the truck with a rejection slip that says which box was wrong: "fruit: expected mango or berry."

  
Programmers call that packing list a schema. Checking a delivery against it is called decoding.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Effect, Console, Schema } from "effect"

// The packing list: what a crate of fruit SHOULD look like.
const Crate = Schema.Struct({
  fruit: Schema.Literals(["mango", "berry"]),     // the word "mango" or the word "berry"
  count: Schema.Int.check(Schema.isGreaterThan(0)) // a whole number above 0
})

// Same description, second job: a type Ty can read.
type Crate = typeof Crate.Type
// { readonly fruit: "mango" | "berry"; readonly count: number }

// The inspector at the back door.
const inspect = Schema.decodeUnknownEffect(Crate)
// inspect : (delivery: unknown) => Effect<Crate, SchemaError>

const backDoor = (delivery: unknown) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const crate = yield* inspect(delivery)        // check every box first
    yield* Console.log(`✅ on the shelf: ${crate.count} ${crate.fruit}`)
  }).pipe(
    Effect.catchTag("SchemaError", (err) => Console.log(`❌ rejected: ${err.message}`))
  )

const morning = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* backDoor({ fruit: "mango", count: 12 })
  yield* backDoor({ fruit: "banana", count: 12 })
  yield* backDoor(JSON.parse('{ "fruit": "berry", "count": 0 }'))
})

Effect.runPromise(morning)
// ✅ on the shelf: 12 mango
// ❌ rejected: Expected "mango" | "berry"
//   at ["fruit"]
// ❌ rejected: Expected a value greater than 0
//   at ["count"]

  
Read the inspector's card out loud: "You get: a Crate. Can go wrong: SchemaError. Needs: nothing." It's a recipe card like any other, so Effect.catchTag from Lesson 4 works on it. unknown is TypeScript's word for "a sealed box, nobody knows what's inside." The inspector is the only one allowed to open it.


  

    
Be the inspector

    
Here is a delivery written as JSON, the text format most deliveries from the internet use. Edit it, or pick a truck, then press Check. The inspector follows the same packing list as the code above.

    

      
      
      
      
      
      
    

    
    
    

      
      
    

    

  


  
What Ty sees

  
Once a crate is past the door, Ty knows its exact shape and helps you again:


const crate = yield* inspect(delivery)
crate.count + 1              // fine: Ty knows count is a number
crate.colour                 // ❌ Ty: there is no "colour" on the packing list
crate.fruit === "kiwi"       // ❌ Ty: fruit can only be "mango" or "berry"

  
You never wrote type Crate = { ... } by hand. It came from the packing list, so the check and the type can't drift apart.


  
The rejection slip

  
By default the inspector stops at the first wrong box. Ask for { errors: "all" } to get every one:


Effect.runPromise(
  inspect({ fruit: "kiwi", count: 2.5 }, { errors: "all" }).pipe(
    Effect.catchTag("SchemaError", (err) => Console.log(`❌ ${err.message}`))
  )
)
// ❌ Expected "mango" | "berry"
//   at ["fruit"]
// Expected an integer
//   at ["count"]

  
Each line says what was expected, then at says which box. That's the whole slip.


  
Check yourself

  
1. Why can't Ty check the delivery trucks the way Ty checks recipe cards?Ty checks cards before the kitchen opens. Deliveries arrive later, while the kitchen is running, so Ty never sees what's inside them. Something has to check them at the door, at run time.

  
2. Name the two jobs one packing list does.It checks the real delivery at the back door (the runtime check), and it gives Ty the type of a good crate (typeof Crate.Type).

  
3. A delivery arrives as { fruit: "mango", count: "12" }. Does it go on the shelf? Which box is wrong?No. "12" in quotes is words, not a number. The slip says Expected number, at ["count"].

  
4. What's on the "Can go wrong" line of inspect(delivery), and how do you cross it off?SchemaError. Cross it off with Effect.catchTag("SchemaError", ...), just like the named errors in Lesson 4.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • Decoding is outside to inside. Encoding is the reverse trip, inside to outside, for when you send data away (save a file, answer a web request). Schema.encodeEffect(Crate) does it. For this schema both sides look the same; they differ once a schema transforms data, like turning the text "2026-10-11" into a real date. Mention, don't teach.
    • 
      
  • Schema.Struct builds a plain object. Schema.Class builds a class from the same field list, for when you want methods on your crates. Same checking, different container.
    • 
      
  • Schema.TaggedError is the schema-backed cousin of Lesson 4's Data.TaggedError: same _tag, same catchTag, but the error itself has a packing list, so it can be safely sent over a network and checked on the other side. Effect's own guides recommend it for errors in real apps.
    • 
      
  • Extra boxes that aren't on the list are quietly dropped from the result by default. Pass { onExcessProperty: "error" } to reject them instead.
    • 
      
  • Schema.fromJsonString(Crate) checks raw JSON text in one step, including "that wasn't JSON at all" (Expected a valid JSON string). Schema.decodeUnknownSync is the version that throws instead of returning a recipe card; it's for the edges of a program, like runPromise.
    • 
      
  • The slip doesn't repeat the bad value by default, on purpose: deliveries can contain passwords.
    • 
      
  • Kids may have heard of zod or valibot. Same idea, different libraries. Many of them, Effect Schema included, speak a shared format called Standard Schema (Schema.toStandardSchemaV1), so form libraries can use any of them.
    • 
      
  • Grown-up words: this is validation or parsing at a trust boundary. "The back door" is fine.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 11: StreamsLesson 13: Logs and spans →


  





  
Lesson 13

  
The Kitchen Diary

  
A busy kitchen keeps a diary, so that tomorrow you can find out what happened today. Effect's diary lines already know when they were written and which bookmark wrote them. They can carry a sticky note (order #42) on every line, and they can time each step with a stopwatch.


  
The story

  
Maya is back at the counter, and she has a question nobody can answer.

  

    

      
      
"What happened to my smoothie?" Sam made thirty smoothies yesterday. Nobody remembers order #42.

    

    

      
      
So the kitchen starts a diary. Every line: the time, how serious, which bookmark. A sticky note for the order, a stopwatch for the blender.

    

    

      
      
A week later it's slow again. Sam flips to the lines with Maya's sticky note. Mystery solved.

    

  

  
Programmers call the diary a log. Writing one line is logging. (Ty can't help here. Ty checks recipe cards before cooking. The diary is about what happened while cooking.)


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code


import { Effect } from "effect"

const smoothie = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* Effect.log("order received")
  yield* Effect.logWarning("only 2 mangoes left")
  yield* Effect.logError("blender jammed!")
})

Effect.runPromise(smoothie)
// something like:
// [16:20:01.042] INFO (#1): order received
// [16:20:01.043] WARN (#1): only 2 mangoes left
// [16:20:01.043] ERROR (#1): blender jammed!

  
Read one line left to right: the time (hours, minutes, seconds, thousandths), the level (how serious), the bookmark (#1 is the fiber that wrote it), and then your message. Your times and numbers will be different. The shape will be the same.

  
Effect.log is a recipe card too, Effect<void>: nothing can go wrong, needs nothing. It only writes when the recipe runs.


  
Whisper or shout

  
Some lines are whispers, some are shouts. The levels, quietest to loudest: Debug (whisper), Info (normal voice), Warn (watch out), Error (problem!).

  
Effect.logDebug("checking the fridge") is a whisper: it is left out unless you ask for it. You can also turn the volume knob the other way, so only warnings and louder get written. The kitchen supplies that setting, just like it supplied the blender in Lesson 5. Same smoothie as above:


import { References } from "effect"

Effect.runPromise(
  smoothie.pipe(Effect.provideService(References.MinimumLogLevel, "Warn"))
)
// something like:
// [16:20:01.043] WARN (#1): only 2 mangoes left
// [16:20:01.043] ERROR (#1): blender jammed!

  
The recipe did not change. Only the knob did.


  
Sticky notes and stopwatches

  
Two orders at once, two bookmarks. First, the sticky note. Effect.annotateLogs sticks it on every line inside, so you don't have to type "order 42" over and over:


const makeSmoothie = (order: number) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    yield* Effect.log("blending")
    yield* Effect.sleep("100 millis")
    yield* Effect.log("poured 🥤")
  }).pipe(Effect.annotateLogs({ order }))   // 🏷️ sticky note on every line

Effect.runPromise(
  Effect.all([makeSmoothie(41), makeSmoothie(42)], { concurrency: 2 })
)
// something like:
// [16:20:01.042] INFO (#2): blending { order: 41 }
// [16:20:01.043] INFO (#3): blending { order: 42 }
// [16:20:01.144] INFO (#2): poured 🥤 { order: 41 }
// [16:20:01.144] INFO (#3): poured 🥤 { order: 42 }

  
Bookmark #2 cooked order 41 and bookmark #3 cooked order 42. The lines are mixed together, but the sticky notes sort them out.

  
Now the stopwatch. Effect.withLogSpan("blend") starts one when the step begins, and every line inside says how long it has been running:


const blend = Effect.gen(function* () {
  yield* Effect.log("blender on")
  yield* Effect.sleep("120 millis")
  yield* Effect.log("blender off")
}).pipe(Effect.withLogSpan("blend"))        // ⏱️ start the stopwatch

Effect.runPromise(blend)
// something like:
// [16:20:01.042] INFO (#1) blend=1ms: blender on
// [16:20:01.164] INFO (#1) blend=122ms: blender off


  

    
Keep the kitchen diary

    
Two orders cook at once on two bookmarks. Run the kitchen, then flip the knob and the toggles: the same run is redrawn as if they had been set from the start. Order 42 has a bad day.

    

      
      
        
        
        
      
      
      
    

    
Press "Run the kitchen".


    
The timeline (spans): one bar per step, smaller steps tucked under the recipe that ran them.

    
  


  
Spans: drawing the timeline

  
A diary is words. Sometimes you want a picture of the day: a bar for each step, showing when it started and how long it took, with smaller steps tucked under bigger ones. Programmers call one bar a span, and the whole picture a trace.


const blend = Effect.sleep("100 millis").pipe(Effect.withSpan("blend"))
const pour  = Effect.sleep("20 millis").pipe(Effect.withSpan("pour"))

const makeSmoothie = Effect.fn("makeSmoothie")(function* (order: number) {
  yield* blend
  yield* pour
  return `🥤 for order ${order}`
})

Effect.runPromise(makeSmoothie(42)).then(console.log)
// 🥤 for order 42
// (no extra lines print: the spans are for a tracing tool to draw)

  
Effect.withSpan("blend") names one step. Effect.fn("makeSmoothie") is a recipe that takes ingredients (here, the order number) and gets a name tag, which makes a span too. Hook up a tracing tool and it draws:

  

  
Check yourself

  
1. Name three parts of a log line that Effect fills in for you.The time, the level, and the bookmark (fiber) number. Plus sticky notes and the stopwatch, if you asked for them.

  
2. Your diary is too noisy. Do you change the recipe, or turn the knob? Which knob?Turn the knob: References.MinimumLogLevel. The recipe stays the same.

  
3. Two smoothies are being made at once and their lines are mixed up. What tells them apart?The bookmark number, like #2 and #3, and the sticky note, like { order: 42 }.

  
4. What's the difference between withLogSpan (stopwatch) and withSpan (a bar on the timeline)?withLogSpan puts a time inside diary lines, like blend=122ms. withSpan makes a bar for a tracing tool to draw on a timeline.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • "Why not just console.log?" console.log has no time, no level, no bookmark, no sticky notes, and you can't turn it down without deleting lines. Unit 1 used Console.log for plain output, and that's still fine for "here is my answer." Effect.log is for "here is what happened."
    • 
      
  • Also: Effect.logFatal (louder than Error), Effect.logTrace (quieter than Debug). Effect.log is Info level. Effect.log("blending", order) takes several values, like console.log, but sticky notes are better for things you want to search by later.
    • 
      
  • The default format is for people. Real apps often switch to one JSON object per line, Logger.layer([Logger.consoleJson]), so machines can search the diary. Mention, don't teach.
    • 
      
  • Tracing tools speak a shared language called OpenTelemetry. Effect ships exporters in effect/observability (OtlpTracer, OtlpLogger). Setting one up needs a running collector; not worth class time. Say "the bars get sent to a tool that draws them."
    • 
      
  • Effect also has metrics (Metric.counter, Metric.histogram): numbers like "smoothies made today." Diary = what happened, timeline = how long, metrics = how many.
    • 
      
  • Fiber numbers like #2 depend on how many fibers ran before, so never test against them. Lesson 14 tests behavior, not diary formatting.
    • 
    

  


  
← Lesson 12: SchemaLesson 14: Testing →


  





  
Lesson 14

  
The Practice Kitchen

  
A recipe card only asks for its appliances and its clock, so you can run it in a practice kitchen with pretend ones. In the practice kitchen the blender is pretend and the wall clock only moves when you turn its knob. A test of "wait 10 minutes, then try again" finishes in a blink.


  
The story

  
Back in Lesson 5, Sam learned recipes in a practice kitchen with a pretend blender. Now the practice kitchen gets one more strange thing.

  

    

      
      
The pretend blender. It says "whirrr" and hands back a smoothie right away. No mess, no real mangoes.

    

    

      
      
The magic wall clock. Its hands only move when someone turns the knob. Ten minutes pass in no time at all.

    

    

      
      
Ty checks the clipboard. A practice run with a checklist is a test. The magic clock is the test clock.

    

  

  
Why want a clock that doesn't move? Look at Lesson 8's routine: "No mango? Check the fridge again every 5 minutes." To practice that with a real clock, Sam would stand around for 10 minutes. With the magic clock, the teacher turns the knob, click, click, and it's done. Ty, the kitchen manager, watches each practice run and checks the result against what it should be: thumbs up or thumbs down.


  
The picture

  

  
The tiniest code

  
Step 1: install the practice kitchen once, in your class folder.


npm install -D vitest @effect/vitest

  
Step 2: make a file whose name ends in .test.ts, like kitchen.test.ts. Bring back Lesson 5's Blender, smoothie, and FakeBlender, then write a test:


import { it, expect } from "@effect/vitest"
import { Effect } from "effect"

it.effect("makes a smoothie with a pretend blender", () =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const drink = yield* smoothie.pipe(Effect.provide(FakeBlender))
    expect(drink).toBe("🥤 (pretend)")
  }))

  
Read it as: "It makes a smoothie with a pretend blender. Run this recipe in the practice kitchen. Expect the drink to be a pretend smoothie." expect is Ty with his clipboard.

  
Step 3: a test that needs the magic clock.


import { Fiber } from "effect"
import { TestClock } from "effect/testing"

it.effect("the toast is ready after 10 minutes", () =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const toast = Effect.sleep("10 minutes").pipe(Effect.as("🍞"))

    const bookmark = yield* Effect.forkChild(toast)   // start it, keep a bookmark
    yield* TestClock.adjust("10 minutes")             // turn the knob
    const result = yield* Fiber.join(bookmark)        // wait for the bookmark

    expect(result).toBe("🍞")
  }))

  
Why the bookmark (Lesson 6)? If Sam just slept on the toast, he would be the one stuck waiting, and nobody would be left to turn the knob. So he starts the toast on a bookmark, turns the knob himself, then picks the bookmark back up.

  
Step 4: run it.


npx vitest run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Duration  313ms

  
Three tests (the third one is below), and the whole run took about a third of a second, even though the recipes "waited" 20 minutes.


  
Fast-forwarding Lesson 8's routine

  
Here is a fridge check that fails twice, then finds a mango. Lesson 8's routine says: try again every 5 minutes.


import { Data, Schedule } from "effect"

class NoMango extends Data.TaggedError("NoMango") {}

it.effect("the fridge check retries every 5 minutes", () =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    let tries = 0
    const checkFridge = Effect.gen(function* () {
      tries = tries + 1
      if (tries < 3) return yield* Effect.fail(new NoMango())
      return "🥭"
    })

    const patient = checkFridge.pipe(Effect.retry(Schedule.spaced("5 minutes")))
    const bookmark = yield* Effect.forkChild(patient)

    yield* TestClock.adjust("5 minutes")
    expect(tries).toBe(2)                     // second try, still no mango

    yield* TestClock.adjust("5 minutes")
    const fruit = yield* Fiber.join(bookmark)
    expect(fruit).toBe("🥭")                  // third try worked
    expect(tries).toBe(3)
  }))

  
Each turn of the knob lets exactly one more try happen. You can stop between turns and check on things, like freezing a video to look at one frame.


  

    
Real clock or test clock?

    
Run the fridge-retry test both ways. The real clock is scaled down here (1 kitchen minute = 0.6 real seconds), or you'd be waiting 10 whole minutes. Watch the stopwatch.

    

      
      
    

    

      
      

    

  


  
Why the clock can be magic

  
Effect.sleep and every schedule from Lesson 8 never look at the wall themselves. They ask Effect's clock what time it is. The clock is an appliance, just like the blender. The kitchen always has one, so it doesn't show up on the "Needs" line, but the recipe still asks for it.

  
Effect.runPromise hands out the real clock. it.effect hands out the test clock. That's the whole trick, and it's the same trick as Lesson 5: the recipe asks, the kitchen provides.


  
Check yourself

  
1. In the practice kitchen, what's pretend? Name two things.The blender (a pretend layer we provide) and the clock (the test clock that it.effect hands out).

  
2. Why does the toast test start the toast on a bookmark (Effect.forkChild) before turning the knob?If the test itself slept, it would be stuck waiting and nothing would be left to turn the knob. The bookmark lets the toast wait while the test keeps going.

  
3. The retry test "waits" 10 minutes. About how long does it really take to run? Why?A few milliseconds. The test clock jumps forward when you call TestClock.adjust; it never ticks through the minutes.

  
4. A friend's recipe calls JavaScript's own setTimeout instead of Effect.sleep. Will TestClock.adjust speed it up?No. setTimeout never asks Effect's clock, so the knob can't reach it. Only waits that ask the kitchen's clock can be fast-forwarded.


  

    Teacher notes
    
    
      
  • If a student forgets TestClock.adjust, the test doesn't fail right away. It sits waiting on a clock that never moves until vitest gives up ("Test timed out in 5000ms"). That's a great bug to make on purpose.
    • 
      
  • it.live("name", () => ...) is the same as it.effect but uses the real clock. Mention it for things that truly need real time; most tests shouldn't.
    • 
      
  • layer(FakeBlender)("practice kitchen", (it) => { ... }) from @effect/vitest gives every test inside the block the same pretend blender, built once. Mention it, don't teach it.
    • 
      
  • expect comes from vitest itself; @effect/vitest passes it along. assert.strictEqual(a, b) works too, and you'll see it in Effect's own examples.
    • 
      
  • This is why services exist. A recipe that builds its own blender, or reads the real clock, can only be practiced in the real kitchen. Asking instead of grabbing is what makes recipes testable.
    • 
      
  • Grown-up terms: a pretend service is a test double (or "fake"); the magic clock is virtual time.
    • 
      
  • Setup: in the class folder, npm install -D vitest @effect/vitest, name files *.test.ts, run npx vitest run (or npx vitest to re-run on every save). No config file is needed.
    • 
      
  • Capstone idea: give students their smoothie shop from Unit 1 and ask for three tests: the happy path with a pretend blender, the "out of mango" path, and a retry that needs the knob turned twice.
    •

Reference

  
Promise vs. Effect, on one page

  
Everything from the fourteen lessons, side by side. The receipt on the left, the recipe card on the right.

  

    

      
QuestionPromise (the receipt)Effect (the recipe card)

      
        
What is it?A value that isn't ready yetA plan for getting a value

        
When does it start?The moment you make itOnly when you run it

        
Can you run it twice?No. One receipt, one smoothieYes, as many times as you like

        
Does the type say what can go wrong?No: Promise<Smoothie>Yes: Effect<Smoothie, OutOfMango>

        
Does the type say what it needs?NoYes: Effect<Smoothie, OutOfMango, Blender>

        
Can you cancel it?NoYes. Interrupt the fiber; cleanup still runs

        
Write steps top to bottomasync / awaitEffect.gen / yield*

        
"Do this when it succeeds".then(f)Effect.map / Effect.andThen

        
"Do this if it fails".catch(f), catches everything, mystery boxEffect.catchTag("Name", f) for one error, Effect.catch for all listed errors

        
Try again on failureWrite a loop yourselfEffect.retry(card, { times: 3 })

        
Give up after a whileHard: a second Promise and a timerEffect.timeout(card, "2 seconds")

        
Several at oncePromise.all([...])Effect.all([...], { concurrency: n })

        
First one winsPromise.race([...]), loser keeps runningEffect.race(a, b), loser is interrupted

        
Always clean uptry { } finally { }, no interrupt caseEffect.acquireRelease: success, error, and interrupt

        
Ask for a helperImport it or pass it in by handyield* Blender, then Effect.provide(layer)

        
Turn it into the other(a Promise is already running)Effect.runPromise(card) at the door of the program

        
Go again on a timetablesetInterval, or a loop with setTimeoutEffect.repeat(card, Schedule.spaced("10 minutes"))

        
Retry, waiting longer each timeA loop, a counter, and setTimeout, by handEffect.retry(card, Schedule.max([Schedule.exponential("1 second"), Schedule.recurs(3)]))

        
Share a number between running tasksA global let; read, await, write back loses updatesRef.make(0), then Ref.update(board, (n) => n + 1), one step

        
Hand work from one task to anotherA shared array and pollingQueue.bounded(3), Queue.offer, Queue.take; a full shelf makes the putter wait

        
Many values over timeEvent listeners push whether you're ready or notStream with map, filter, take; runs only when pulled

        
Check data from outsideJSON.parse and hopeSchema.decodeUnknownEffect(Crate)(data) gives Effect<Crate, SchemaError>

        
Write down what happenedconsole.log: no time, level, or fiberEffect.log, Effect.annotateLogs({ order: 42 }), Effect.withLogSpan("blend")

        
Test "wait 10 minutes" quicklyFake timers that patch setTimeout everywhereit.effect + TestClock.adjust("10 minutes")

      
    

  


  
Reading an Effect type out loud

  
Effect<Smoothie, OutOfMango, Blender>

  
"An Effect that gives you a Smoothie, might fail with OutOfMango, and needs a Blender."

  
    
    
  • never in slot 2: nothing can go wrong.
    • 
    
  • never in slot 3: needs nothing. Ready to run.
    • 
    
  • Trailing nevers can be left off: Effect<number> means Effect<number, never, never>.
    • 
  


  
The five lines of Unit 1 you actually need


import { Effect, Console, Context, Layer, Data, Fiber } from "effect"

Effect.gen(function* () { const x = yield* step; return x })   // a recipe with steps
class OutOfMango extends Data.TaggedError("OutOfMango") {}     // a named error
class Blender extends Context.Service<Blender, { ... }>()("Blender") {}   // a needed thing
Layer.succeed(Blender, { ... })                                 // a way to provide it
Effect.runPromise(card.pipe(Effect.provide(layer)))            // the door out of the kitchen


  
The Unit 2 lines you'll reach for


import { Effect, Schedule, Ref, Queue, Stream, Schema } from "effect"
import { TestClock } from "effect/testing"

Effect.retry(card, Schedule.exponential("1 second"))               // try again, waiting longer each time
Ref.make(0)                                                        // a card that makes a shared whiteboard
Queue.bounded<string>(3)                                           // a card that makes a 3-slot order shelf
Stream.make("🥭", "🍓", "🥝").pipe(Stream.map(wash), Stream.take(2))  // a conveyor belt with stations
Schema.decodeUnknownEffect(Crate)(delivery)                        // check the delivery at the back door
Effect.log("blending").pipe(Effect.annotateLogs({ order: 42 }))    // a diary line with a sticky note
TestClock.adjust("10 minutes")                                     // turn the magic clock's knob


  
Kitchen word, programmer word

  

    

      
Kitchen pictureProgrammer wordWhat it means

      
        
One cooksingle-threadedJavaScript does one instruction at a time. Always.

        
Standing and staring at the toasterblocking / synchronousWaiting in a way that freezes everything else.

        
Leaving a ticket and walking awayasynchronousWaiting in a way that lets other work happen.

        
The ticket you leavecallbackA function to run later, when something finishes.

        
The ticket railevent loopThe list the cook checks whenever hands are free.

        
A receipt for a smoothiePromiseA value that isn't ready yet. Starts the moment it's made.

        
A recipe cardEffectA plan for producing a value. Does nothing until run.

        
"You get" / "Can go wrong" / "Needs"Success / Error / RequirementsThe three slots of the Effect type.

        
Nothing on that lineneverNothing can go wrong, or nothing is needed.

        
Out of mangoerrorA known failure, written on the card, must be handled.

        
Kitchen firedefectA bug. Not on the card. Crashes loudly on purpose.

        
A name tag on a problemtagged errorAn error class with a _tag string.

        
An appliance the recipe asks forserviceA described capability, like "a Blender that can blend."

        
The kitchen supplying the appliancelayerA way to build or provide a service.

        
Ty, the kitchen managerthe type checkerReads every card before it can run. Stops incomplete ones.

        
A bookmark in a half-done recipefiberA running Effect that can be paused, resumed, or stopped.

        
Pulling the bookmark outinterruptionStopping a fiber cleanly; its cleanup still runs.

        
Borrow it, always return itacquire / releaseGet a resource and guarantee cleanup on every ending.

        
The due datescopeThe window during which a borrowed resource is held.

        
The routine chart on the wallscheduleA plan for when to go again and when to stop, separate from any card.

        
Knock again / wipe againretry / repeatGo again after a failure / go again after a success, following a schedule.

        
The kitchen whiteboardRefOne shared value; Ref.update reads, changes, and writes it back in one step.

        
Three sales, board says 1lost update (race condition)A fiber reads, pauses, and writes back an old number.

        
The order shelfqueueValues between fibers, first in, first out. Waits when empty or full.

        
The full shelf pushing backbackpressureA slow taker makes a fast putter wait.

        
A conveyor belt of fruitstreamMany values, one after another, maybe forever. Moves only when pulled.

        
The packing list by the back doorschemaDescribes good data once: checks it while running, and gives Ty the type.

        
The rejection slipSchemaErrorWhat's on the "Can go wrong" line when a delivery doesn't match.

        
The kitchen diarylogA line with the time, the level, and the bookmark that wrote it.

        
A sticky note / a stopwatchannotation / log spanExtra info on every line / how long a step has been running.

        
One bar on the timelinespanA named step with a start and an end, for a tracing tool to draw.

        
The practice kitchentestRun a recipe with pretend appliances and check the result.

        
The magic wall clocktest clockA clock that only moves when the test turns the knob.
